projectOutComesReport:
Research Questions

Many people have strong opinions about the kind of person they want to mate with or marry, and we spend a lot of time evaluating potential partners for these qualities. These time-consuming tasks likely have an evolutionary function—they steer us toward mates that have qualities that will increase our reproductive success. While this assumption has been experimentally tested in animals, the same experimental methods are not possible in humans. Instead, we have to rely on existing cultural systems where there is variation in the amount of independent mate choice individuals exercise. One such case is arranged marriages, a common system across cultures in which parents are deeply involved in choosing a partner for their offspring, sometimes with little input from the marrying individuals. Evidence indicates that parents arranging a marriage are not evaluating sons- or daughters-in-law based on the same qualities that offspring would use to find a match on their own. Therefore, individuals in arranged marriages, who are not fully expressing their mate preferences, should have reduced reproductive success, but our previous work examining this prediction does not find any differences between couples in arranged and non-arranged marriages. This project explores the reasons behind these results.

 

Study Site

We collected data from over 1,000 individuals in Dhading, Nepal, an area rapidly transitioning from a traditional system of parentally arranged marriages to self-chosen marriages with less parental involvement. In Nepal, we hired a team of local research assistants who received training on data collection and management. Some of these local researchers used that experience to secure jobs or admission to educational programs.

 

Measuring Preferences in a Marriage Partner

To investigate why previous studies of arranged and non-arranged marriages have similar reproductive outcomes, we first examined divergence between the in-law/partner preferences of parents and offspring in Dhading, Nepal. Over 700 participants allocated a budget to a set of 14 traits to design their ideal spouse (for unmarried respondents) or in-law (for parents of unmarried adults). By comparing the budget allocated to each trait by parents and unmarried individuals, we quantified the overall amount of disagreement and identified the traits causing that disagreement. We measured substantial disagreement between parents and offspring, and this disagreement was most pronounced in traits like physical attractiveness (preferred by offspring) and caste identity (preferred by parents). This portion of the project provided training for one undergraduate at UC Santa Barbara, who gained valuable data skills and coding experience in R Statistical Software.

 

Cultural Context of Arranged Marriage

We then examined the cultural context of arranged marriages in Nepal via 17 focus groups. First, these focus groups demonstrated that there are three categories of marriage in the local community—arranged marriages, love marriages, and elopements—each of which encompass varying levels of parent and offspring involvement. Second, we found a strong desire from parents and offspring to work together on selecting a spouse in an arranged marriage. Even though the budget allocation task (above) highlighted disagreement, these focus groups showed room for compromise and collaboration. Lastly, these focus groups identified several social and financial incentives tied to arranged marriages that make these an attractive option for many individuals. For example, arranged marriages provide more family support in cases of marital conflict, and arranged marriages come with substantial marital gifts. These benefits were larger for women than for men, indicating that women in this community may have substantial incentives to enter arranged marriages. For this project, we worked with two undergraduate researchers at UC Santa Barbara who coded and analyzed the focus group transcripts. These undergraduates, plus a local Nepali researcher, are coauthors on the publication.

 

Importance

These results highlight the role of kin and social support in human mating, and may explain why previous studies examining the relationship between mate choice and reproductive outcomes did not find the predicted results. This role of kin and social networks in mate choice may be unique among animals.

 

Remaining Projects

This grant supported two additional research objectives for which data was collected in Nepal during the grant period. These data have been prepared for analysis and will be analyzed in the next year. We will examine whether reproductive outcomes differ for individuals in different types of marriages (our initial hypothesis) using a more dynamic measure of spouse choice. Second, we will explore the reasons for any reproductive differences (or lack thereof) by analyzing data on grandparental support, marital gift giving, inheritances, and perceived social support to examine the costs and benefits of parental involvement in marriage decisions. During collection of these data, which included child height, weight, and body fat measurements, participants received reports of their health data to assist them in making healthcare decisions. Summative results of these analyses will also be shared with the local health clinic to help target child health programs in the communities.

abstractText:
An animal's nervous system controls its behavior.  Complex behavioral sequences are assembled from simpler motor programs.  Like nest-building in birds and web-spinning in spiders, grooming in flies represents a flexible, innate, adaptive motor sequence.  This project will use the genetic tools available in flies, combined with new machine vision analysis, to identify the neurons that control fly grooming behavior.  It will focus on the connections between the brain and the ventral nervous system, since these descending neurons are a natural information bottleneck.  Understanding how a limited number of neurons convey commands and coordinate competing reflexes into productive behaviors will advance basic knowledge in neuroscience and provide conceptual insights into how any brain – including human ones – solve similar challenges.  One focus of the NSF's mission to promote basic science research is to understand the rules of life, and specifically to predict phenotypes.  This research contributes to ongoing efforts to generate maps of all the neurons and their connections in the fly by adding information about their behavioral functions. As part of the educational objectives of this project, the PI will organize a summer course at the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics for experimentalists and theorists that will involve both cutting edge topics in modern systems neuroscience and theoretical approaches. Specific efforts will be made to recruit undergraduate students to this quantitative biology summer course. 

This research will employ automated behavioral analysis of Drosophila grooming, optogenetic manipulations, and anatomical characterization of neuronal circuits.  Screens using new genetic reagents to target specific descending neurons will delineate their behavioral roles.  The project will characterize the projections and connections of these neurons to determine how they interface with sensory and motor circuits.  Activating combinations of descending neurons that initiate competing behavioral programs will reveal whether decisions are made in the brain or the ventral nerve cord.  Neural circuits that can be mapped in the fly represent fundamental motifs that perform computations common to all brains.  Understanding their roles in grooming behavior uses the advantages of this model to learn how the brain achieves motor sequences. The broader impact activities include a summer laboratory course in systems neuroscience as part of the ongoing KITP summer program in quantitative biology as well as undergraduate and graduate student training.

program: CAREER-Faculty Erly Career Dev, NEURAL SYSTEMS, UNITED KINGDOM, UNDERGRADUATE EDUCATION, GRADUATE INVOLVEMENT
projectOutComesReport:
Understanding how the nervous system coordinates appropriate behaviors is a challenge relevant to human health that we can investigate with basic science research in model organisms.  Neurons connecting the brain to the ventral nerve cord in the adult fly Drosophila represent a control bottleneck.  Sensory information and internal drives coordinated in the brain activate specific combinations of descending neurons to convey decisions about appropriate behavioral responses to the pre-motor circuits in the ventral cord that execute movements.  New genetic tools allow descending neurons to be activated or silenced to assess their behavioral effects, and new anatomical datasets allow their synaptic, network connections with other neurons to be mapped.

In this project, we identified descending neurons that can initiate different cleaning movements like those that normally remove dirt and debris from the fly’s body and we investigated how different combinations of neurons control assembly of individual cleaning movements into the sequential, coordinated grooming.  We showed that antennal cleaning, head cleaning, and front leg rubbing can be initiated separately or as alternating subroutines by different command-like descending neurons, allowing for both rhythmic and more flexibly targeted grooming.  Activating multiple descending neurons does not make the flies do two behaviors at once, showing that circuits for action selection are located downstream.  This demonstrates that modular and redundant control mechanisms may underlie motor sequence assembly. 

We characterized the GABAergic, inhibitory neurons that receive indirect synaptic input from descending neurons and coordinate pre-motor circuits within and between the legs.  Comprehensive anatomical and behavioral investigation of these neural types shows that they complement excitatory neurons to provide an alternative way to group which muscles co-contract, creating the muscle synergies and motor primitives that are the repeated building blocks of coordinated limb movements.  Some inhibitory neurons connect to many pre-motor neurons while others connect to only a few, suggesting a way that core leg movements can be tuned for grooming or walking.

Some types of neurons have “serial homologs”: anatomically similar neurons in each segment to the ventral nerve cord.  We identified a set of six ascending neurons, two per segment, whose activation evokes leg rubbing in behavioral screens.  These neurons have projections ascending from the ventral nerve cord to the brain, and there is a pair of descending neurons with similar connectivity that we discovered in the connectome data.  Differences in the commissural projections of the circuits connected to these neurons in the middle segment may explain why flies groom those body parts with a distinct combination of legs.

These experimental results illuminate the organizational logic that allows a small population of neurons to control a complex, flexible, and sequential repertoire of movements, providing a template to which the neural control of motor sequences in vertebrates can be compared.  

The research supported by this award informed teaching and outreach efforts, notably influencing the choice of topics for two summer programs hosted by the UCSB KITP, the neurophysics of locomotion (2022) and the coming neurophysics of active sensing (2025).  These programs and the associated quantitative biology schools bring experimentalists and theorists together for a month-long opportunity for collaboration and cross-training, exposing students and senior investigators to different ways of approaching questions in neuroscience.

abstractText:
Skeletal remains are important sources of information on temporal trends in human health. Porous cranial lesions (PCLs) are interpreted as indicators of nutrient deficiencies and chronic infections and are among the most common pathological findings in human skeletal remains. This doctoral dissertation project uses methods previously applied primarily in archaeological contexts to investigating the causes of PCLs and the health of individuals who live with them. Specifically, the researchers will use an archaeological reference sample to develop computed tomography (CT) criteria for identifying PCLs in living individuals. They will then link measures of individual health to PCL findings from existing CT scans of a living population. Protocols and tools developed for PCL analysis will be made freely available online. The project will strengthen institutional capacity for future research collaborations and support STEM student training at the graduate and undergraduate levels. Because PCLs are developed during childhood, the methods developed in this proposal will have implications for public health across the lifespan. 

PCLs in archaeological samples have been interpreted as evidence of both stress and resilience. This project attempts to resolve this ambiguity by leveraging existing data drawn from a living population to test the association of PCLs in the orbits (cribra orbitalia) and the cranial vault (porotic hyperostosis) with known health profiles. First, the researchers will develop a protocol to extend archaeological methods to determining the prevalence of PCLs in a living population. Specifically, investigators will employ both visual assessments of CT scans and machine learning to reliably identify the presence and extent of PCLs on cranial CT scans using a reference sample of archaeological crania (n = 600). Once developed, investigators will apply the protocol to identify PCLs on existing cranial CTs of 1,310 living adults with known health profiles. This will link childhood development of PCLs to measures of later life health, including biological markers, medical diagnoses, and self-reported wellness. Finally, this project tests the common interpretation of PCLs as indicators of childhood anemia. Using biological markers from dried blood spot samples from children in the same population of living individuals (n = 480), investigators will identify the underlying causes of individual anemia cases and test their association with a biological marker of active bone remodeling.

projectOutComesReport:
This project was the first study to examine porous cranial lesions in the bones of the orbits (cribra orbitalia) and cranial vault (cribra cranii) in a population-representative sample of living people. These lesions are commonly reported by archaeologists as skeletal indicators of childhood stress, who attribute them to either infectious or nutritional causes in early life.

We first tested the sensitivity and accuracy of clinical computed tomography scans for identifying cranial lesions in living people by scanning archaeological crania with a range of lesion presentations. We found that moderate to severe cases of cranial porosity could be reliably documented from CT scans using settings intended to diagnose cranial fractures.  

We then evaluated existing head scans of adults aged 40+ years from the Tsimane population of Bolivia for cranial lesions presumably developed in early childhood. Using twenty years of health data from the Tsimane Health and Life History Project, we investigated the relationship between 1) cranial lesions and childhood health and 2) cranial lesions and morbidity in later life.

We found that cranial lesions were not associated with other measures of childhood illness or growth disruption (memories of childhood sickness; leg length relative to total height). However, we do find that shared childhood household is an independent predictor of lesion status, supporting the idea that childhood environment plays a role in the development of these skeletal lesions.

There is some evidence that cribra orbitalia is associated with immunocompromise in Tsimane adults, suggesting lifelong health consequences of lesion-causing processes in early life. Cribra orbitalia is associated with lower measures for some markers of adaptive immunity (fewer B cells, na?ve CD4+ T cells, and a lower ratio of total CD4+ T cells to CD8+ T cells) and with a greater risk of developing active tuberculosis. Cribra cranii, on the other hand, predicts double the risk of headaches but is not associated with notable differences in physiological measures.

We also assayed dried blood spots from Tsimane children for measures of iron deficiency (serum transferrin receptor), inflammation (C-reactive protein), and skeletal activity (osteocalcin) to investigate relationships between nutrient deficiency, infection, and processes of skeletal change during childhood. At the time of writing analyses are still underway, but initial explorations show a negative relationship between iron levels and skeletal activity, perhaps suggesting that childhood anemia, a known cause of cranial changes, is not the predominant cause of porous cranial lesions in this population.

The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is to commercialize smart compression garments for enhancing performance gains during fitness, athletic training, and rehabilitation.  The products to be commercialized are intended to address important needs in health and training that may be of interest to many fitness enthusiasts, amateur or professional athletes, and individuals recovering from physical challenges. This could include millions of individuals in the United States.  The potential benefits for society and the economy are commensurately high.  In the long term, this project may hold benefits for a large number of individuals that personally or professionally engage in physically demanding activities in the workplace, or that require physical assistance for activities of daily living. The underlying technology holds the potential to enable applications in healthcare and assistive and rehabilitative devices that could improve quality of life.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of a fabric technology that consists of a soft, muscle-like robotic fabric, that uses an actuated composite polymer textile.  These actuated textiles consist of composite fabric structures that integrate an elastic-hydraulic transmission. Previous research revealed that the textiles are capable of supplying large, dynamic forces or displacements via soft fabrics that may be fashioned into wearable garments, which may be fabricated using facile textile manufacturing methods. This technology holds the potential to enable a wide variety of wearable garments with applications in fitness, healthcare, and many other areas.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
This NSF I-Corps Project was directed at commercializing smart compression garments for increasing the gains that athletes experience during training. Findings from the project, obtained through extensive mentoring by I-Corps staff and via interviews with more than 100 stakeholders, highlight the important needs this product and technology could meet in supporting the activities of thousands of athletes, stakeholders, and teams, both professional and amateur.  During the course of the project, the team was able to select a sector of athletics that was determined to be most suitable for initial commercialization activities, based on a combination of unmet needs reported by stakeholders and economic analyses.  The number of individual beneficiaries and the economic dimensions, as analyzed during the project, further highlight the large potential benefits for society and the economy that could results from this commercialization activity.  Future devices similar to the one the team aims to commercialize, also enabled by the technology that this project was focused on, have significant potential broader impacts through their application in related areas of great societal and economic significance.  These include potential applications for improving rehabilitation of injuries sustained by millions of athletes and non-athletes each year, thus reducing costs and improving quality of life for many individuals.

This I-Corps project was directed at commercializing a fabric technology previously developed in the lab of the principal investigator. This fabric technology enables soft, muscle-like robotic textiles that integrate an elastic-hydraulic transmission. Previous research revealed that the textiles are capable of supplying large, dynamic forces or displacements via soft fabrics that may be fashioned into wearable garments, which may be fabricated using facile textile manufacturing methods. This technology holds the potential to enable a wide variety of wearable garments with applications in fitness, healthcare, and many other areas.
